Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
The current landscape of adapting Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) faces a critical dichotomy between performance and efficiency. While full fine-tuning offers robust zero-shot generalization, it is computationally prohibitive given the escalating scale of foundation models. Conversely, existing Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods (such as adapters or weight reparameterization) often fail to close the performance gap with full fine-tuning. Furthermore, current PEFT approaches operate as "black boxes," modifying abstract model weights in a way that is detached from the physical and semantic characteristics of the data. This lack of interpretability limits our ability to understand or explicitly control model behavior during the adaptation process.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that directly editing the **semantic representations** (the data flowing through the network) is a more effective and efficient strategy than modifying the model parameters (the weights). We posit that task-specific knowledge and instruction adherence can be injected by learning lightweight, linear interventions on the feature maps themselves. By manipulating these representations within a low-rank subspace, we believe we can steer the model's behavior with extreme parameter sparsity while retaining—and potentially exceeding—the performance of weight-based tuning methods.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose a framework for **Multimodal Representation Tuning (MRT)**. Our strategy involves freezing the entire pre-trained LMM backbone and exclusively training a set of "Representation Editors" inserted at strategic points in the data flow.

*   **Representation Editors:** Instead of standard adapter layers that process outputs, we will design editors based on the linear representation hypothesis. These modules will function by projecting the incoming feature representation into a low-rank subspace, computing a learned "intervention" (a shift in values), and adding this intervention back to the original representation. This allows us to "steer" the features without altering the original model weights.

*   **Holistic Intervention Strategy:** We plan to apply these editors across the entire multimodal pipeline to ensure coherent adaptation:
    1.  **Visual Representation:** We will insert editors into the layers of the Vision Encoder to adjust how visual features are extracted and processed before they reach the language model.
    2.  **Cross-Modality Alignment:** We will place an editor at the projection layer (the interface between vision and language) to refine the alignment between visual embeddings and the LLM's input space.
    3.  **Multimodal/Textual Representation:** Within the Large Language Model itself, we will specifically target the textual-oriented embeddings. We aim to edit the representations of instruction prefixes and suffixes, thereby guiding the generation process through context manipulation.

*   **Intervention Flow:** The process will be strictly feed-forward. The editor takes the current layer's activation, applies the learned offset, and passes the modified representation to the next frozen layer. This decouples visual and textual editing, potentially allowing for more precise control over specific modalities.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Extreme Parameter Efficiency:** We expect to achieve state-of-the-art adaptation performance with a fraction of the trainable parameters required by current methods (e.g., LoRA), as we are modifying low-rank activations rather than high-dimensional weight matrices.
2.  **Bridging the Performance Gap:** We aim to demonstrate that representation editing can rival or surpass full fine-tuning capabilities by leveraging the rich semantic information already present in the pre-trained activations.
3.  **Interpretability and Control:** By establishing a direct link between representation interventions and model output, this approach effectively introduces a mechanism for "white-box" control. We anticipate this will allow for predictable manipulation of model behavior (e.g., inducing counterfactuals) simply by adjusting the intervention vectors, offering a new perspective on LMM transparency.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

### Model Architecture & Configuration
*   **Base Model:** Stage-one LLaVA.
*   **Vision Encoder:** CLIP-L (24 Transformer-based encoder layers).
*   **Large Language Model (Backbone):** Vicuna-7B-v1.3 (32 Transformer-based decoder layers).
*   **Cross-Modality:** Pre-trained cross-modality projector connecting the second-last layer of the vision encoder to the LLM.
*   **Method:** Multimodal Representation Tuning (MRT).
    *   **Visual Representation Editing:** Applied to the entire visual representation in CLIP-L and the cross-modality layer.
    *   **Multimodal Representation Editing:** Applied to textual-oriented prefixes and suffixes in Vicuna-7B-v1.3.
    *   **Tunable Parameters:** Only representation editors were updated; the entire base model remained frozen.
    *   **Parameter Count:** 0.03% of total model parameters.

### Training Implementation
*   **Hardware:** NVIDIA A100-40GB GPUs.
*   **Framework:** PyTorch.
*   **Optimizer:** Adam.
*   **Learning Rate:** 6e-4.
*   **Batch Size:** 128.
*   **Epochs:** 3 (for main instruction tuning), 1 (for controllability experiments).
*   **LR Scheduler:** Linear with Warmup Ratio 0.03.
*   **Precision:** bfloat16 activation type.
*   **Initialization:** Orthogonal initialization for low-rank matrix $U$; standard linear layer initialization for linear projector $W$.

### Datasets
*   **Training Dataset:** Vision-Flan (scaled-down version).
    *   **Size:** 191,105 instances total (up to 1,000 instances per task).
    *   **Diversity:** 191 distinct multimodal tasks.
*   **Evaluation Benchmarks (Zero-shot):**
    *   **MME:** Comprehensive benchmark measuring Perception (Existence, Count, Position, Color, Poster, Celebrity, Scene, Landmark, Artwork, OCR) and Cognition (Commonsense reasoning, Numerical calculation, Text translation, Code reasoning).
    *   **Text-VQA:** Optical Character Recognition.
    *   **VSR (Visual Spatial Reasoning):** Spatial reasoning.
    *   **SNLI-VE:** Visual Entailment.
    *   **CIFAR-10:** Visual Perception.
    *   **CIFAR-100:** Visual Perception.
    *   **MNIST:** Visual Perception.
    *   **POPE:** Object Hallucination tendencies.
    *   **SEED-Bench:** Generative comprehension (Appendix experiment).
    *   **GQA:** Visual reasoning (Appendix experiment).

### Evaluation Metrics
*   **MME:** Sum of accuracy values across 14 subtasks (Perception + Cognition).
*   **Other Multimodal Datasets (Text-VQA, VSR, etc.):** Accuracy.
    *   **Judge:** Vicuna-13B-v1.5 was used to assess prediction accuracy against ground truth (judging "Yes" for correct predictions).

### Baselines Compared
*   **LLaVA Align:** Stage-one LLaVA without end-to-end fine-tuning.
*   **LLaVA FT:** Fully fine-tuned LLaVA (100% parameters).
*   **LoRA:** Low-Rank Adaptation (Reparameterization method).
*   **APrompt:** Attention Prompt Tuning (Single modality - textual).
*   **PTUM:** Prompt Tuning for Unified Multimodal models.
*   **VPT:** Visual Prompt Tuning (Single modality - visual).
*   **ReFT:** Representation Finetuning (Textual modality representation tuning).
*   **M²PT:** Multimodal Prompt Tuning.
*   **MixLoRA:** Multimodal instruction tuning with conditional mixture of LoRA.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

### General Performance
*   We achieved 99.56% of the full fine-tuning performance on the MME benchmark while utilizing only 0.03% of the parameters.
*   MRT outperformed all compared PEFT baselines (LoRA, APrompt, PTUM, VPT, ReFT, M²PT, MixLoRA) on the MME benchmark, showing a 4.70% improvement over MixLoRA and 5.08% over M²PT.
*   On specific tasks like Text-VQA, CIFAR-10, and MNIST, MRT surpassed the performance of the fully fine-tuned LLaVA model.
*   PEFT approaches focusing on multimodality (M²PT, MRT) generally outperformed single-modality approaches (APrompt, VPT, ReFT).
*   Performance on the SNLI-VE (Visual Entailment) task was lower compared to other tasks, a trend observed across other PEFT methods like PTUM and M²PT.

### Controllability and Interpretability
*   We successfully demonstrated token-wise representation editing for controllability.
*   **Misclassification Scenario:** We achieved a 100% success rate in forcing the model to misclassify specific classes (e.g., cat, dog) as "No" in binary verification questions, without affecting the classification accuracy of other classes.
*   **Misalignment Scenario:** We achieved a 100% success rate in forcing the model to misalign a specific class into a targeted incorrect class, again maintaining accuracy for non-targeted classes.
*   **Text-VQA Extension:** We successfully controlled the model to answer "Not sure" for specific attributes (name, color, brand) with 100% effectiveness.
*   **Rephrasing Robustness:** Using a T5-small rephraser allowed us to maintain 100% control rates across various prompt phrasings with identical semantic meanings.

### Ablation and Diagnostic Findings
*   **Impact of Rank:**
    *   We observed that performance saturates around rank 8.
    *   The optimal configuration was found to be Visual Rank 6 and Multimodal Rank 4, achieving the peak MME score of 1580.40.
    *   Increasing ranks beyond the optimum (e.g., Visual 8, Multimodal 8) resulted in lower performance (1505.32 on MME), suggesting overparameterization or slower convergence.
*   **Editing Position:**
    *   Removing any single editor component (visual, multimodal, or cross-modality) degraded performance.
    *   Removing the cross-modality editor had the smallest negative impact, while removing visual or multimodal editors caused significant drops.
*   **Editing Length:**
    *   We observed a non-linear relationship between intervention length (prefix/suffix tokens) and performance.
    *   Optimal editing lengths were identified as 4 and 6 for prefixes and suffixes.
    *   Short lengths (e.g., 2) were insufficient, while longer lengths (e.g., 8, 10) degraded performance (MME score dropped to 1213.68 at length 10).
*   **Optimization Landscape:**
    *   Visualizations of the loss landscape showed that MRT produces a flatter loss landscape with a larger connected region around the local minimum compared to MixLoRA and M²PT.
    *   Baselines like MixLoRA exhibited sharper landscapes sensitive to loss fluctuations.
*   **Impact of Editing Depth:**
    *   Performance was positively correlated with editing depth.
    *   Editing the "Latter Half" of layers (MME: 1447.41) performed better than editing the "First Half" (MME: 1440.32).
    *   Sparse editing (Every Odd Layer) outperformed continuous block editing (First/Latter halves), achieving an MME score of 1468.21.

### Efficiency
*   MRT demonstrated faster inference times compared to M²PT (72.73% faster) and MixLoRA (42.86% faster).
*   Training memory usage (16GB) and time (9 hours) were competitive, being lower than LoRA (19GB, 16 hours) and MixLoRA (23GB, 24 hours).

Conference Guidelines
# ICLR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the LaTeX paper writing process for ICLR 2025.

## General Setup
* **Document Class:** `\documentclass{article}`
* **Required Packages:**
    ```latex
    \usepackage{iclr2025_conference,times}
    \usepackage{hyperref}
    \usepackage{url}
    % Optional but recommended for math
    \input{math_commands.tex}
    ```
* **Style Files:** You must use `iclr2025_conference.sty` and `iclr2025_conference.bst`.

## Anonymity (Crucial)
* ICLR is double-blind. **Do not** include real author names or affiliations in the submission version, use "Ambitious AI Researcher" instead.
* Use the third person when citing your own prior work (e.g., "Earlier work by Smalle (2024)..." instead of "In our earlier work...").
* You may post your paper on arXiv, but do not explicitly refer to the arXiv version in the paper to maintain anonymity.

## Paper Length
* **Main Text:** Strict upper limit of **10 pages**.
* **Citations:** Unlimited additional pages.
* **Ethics & Reproducibility Statements:** Optional. Do not count toward the page limit (max 1 page each).
* **Acknowledgments:** Do not count toward the page limit.

## Abstract
The abstract must be limited to **one paragraph**.
* **Margins:** Indented 1/2 inch (3 picas) on both left and right-hand margins.
* **Font:** 10-point type, vertical spacing of 11-points.
* **Title:** The word `\textsc{Abstract}` must be centered, in small caps, and in point size 12.
* **Spacing:** Two line spaces precede the abstract.

## Formatting Your Paper
The text must be confined within a rectangle 5.5 inches (33 picas) wide and 9 inches (54 picas) long. The left margin is 1.5 inch (9 picas).
* **Font:** Times New Roman (via `times` package) is preferred.
* **Size:** 10-point type with 11-point vertical spacing.
* **Paragraphs:** Separated by 1/2 line space, with **no indentation**.
* **Paper Title:** 17-point, small caps, left-aligned.

### Headings
* **First Level:** Small caps (`\textsc`), flush left, 12-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Second Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Third Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.

## Citations and References
Use the `natbib` package (loaded automatically by the style file).
* **Narrative citation:** Use `\citet{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "Gomu et al. (2024)".
* **Parenthetical citation:** Use `\citep{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "(Gomu et al., 2024)".
* **Bibliography:**
    ```latex
    \bibliography{references}
    \bibliographystyle{iclr2025_conference}
    ```

## Figures and Tables
* All artwork must be neat, clean, and legible.
* **Captions:** Lower case (except for first word and proper nouns).
* **Placement:**
    * **Figures:** Caption appears **after** (below) the figure.
    * **Tables:** Caption appears **before** (above) the table.

## Math Notation
* ICLR encourages standardized notation using `\input{math_commands.tex}` (based on the Deep Learning book notation).
* Variables: Italics ($a$, $\va$, $\mA$).
* Random Variables: Roman ($P(\ra)$).
* Sets: Blackboard bold ($\R$, $\sA$).
* Functions: Standard LaTeX ($f(\vx)$).

references.text:
## Problem Statement
The rapid scaling of Large Multimodal Models (LMMs), such as LLaVA and Flamingo, has created a critical bottleneck in model adaptation. Standard full fine-tuning is becoming computationally prohibitive due to the immense parameter count (ranging from 7B to 70B+). While Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) strategies—such as LoRA, Adapters, and Prompt Tuning—have been introduced to mitigate this, they suffer from two primary limitations. First, they exhibit a significant performance gap compared to full fine-tuning while still requiring a non-trivial number of trainable parameters. Second, existing PEFT parameters are often abstract and independent of the physical characteristics of the modeled problem, operating as "black-box" modifications that are difficult to interpret or control. There is currently no framework that leverages the semantically rich internal representations of LMMs for efficient tuning and explicit behavior control.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose **Multimodal Representation Tuning (MRT)**, a novel fine-tuning strategy based on the hypothesis that direct, linear editing of internal representations is superior to weight reparameterization. We posit that by manipulating representations within specific low-rank subspaces, we can achieve zero-shot generalization comparable to full fine-tuning with a fraction of the parameters (targeting $\approx 0.03\%$). Furthermore, we hypothesize that this representation-centric approach will unlock "white-box" controllability, allowing us to steer model behavior and correct misclassifications by explicitly editing instrumental tokens within the visual and multimodal streams.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop a framework that freezes the pre-trained LMM and introduces learnable **Representation Editors** ($\psi$) at strategic points in the architecture: the vision encoder, the cross-modality projector, and the Large Language Model (LLM).

### 1. Base Architecture and Data Flow
We will utilize a standard Transformer-based LMM architecture $\mathcal{F}$ comprising:
*   A vision encoder $\nu$ (e.g., CLIP-L) with hidden dimensionality $d_v$.
*   An LLM $\tau$ (e.g., Vicuna) with hidden dimensionality $d_t$.
*   A linear cross-modality projector $\mathcal{C}$ mapping $d_v \to d_t$.

The input processing flow will be defined as follows:
1.  **Visual Encoding:** Input image $\mathbf{I}$ is encoded into $m$ visual tokens: $T_v = \mathcal{V}(\mathbf{I}) = \{T_v^1, \dots, T_v^m\}$.
2.  **Projection:** Visual tokens are mapped to the LLM space: $X_v = \mathcal{C}(T_v)$.
3.  **Tokenization:** Text instruction $\mathbf{T}$ is tokenized into $n$ tokens: $X_t = \{x_t^1, \dots, x_t^n\}$.
4.  **Fusion:** The joint representation is $X = \mathsf{Concat}(X_v, X_t)$.
5.  **Generation:** The LLM produces response $y = \tau(X)$.

### 2. Mathematical Formulation of the Representation Editor
We will introduce a generic representation editor $\psi$ inspired by the linear representation hypothesis. For a given feature representation $\boldsymbol{x}$, the editor will learn a linear intervention within a low-rank subspace. We formulate the editor $\psi$ as:

$$ \boldsymbol{\psi}(\boldsymbol{x}) = \boldsymbol{x} + \boldsymbol{U}^{\intercal} (\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{x} + \boldsymbol{b} - \boldsymbol{U}\boldsymbol{x}) $$

Where:
*   $\boldsymbol{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_t}$ is the original representation.
*   $\boldsymbol{U} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_l \times d_t}$ is a learnable low-rank matrix with **orthonormal rows**, defining the subspace for editing.
*   $\boldsymbol{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_l \times d_t}$ and $\boldsymbol{b} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_l}$ are learnable parameters defining the linear projection and bias of the target intervention.
*   $d_l \ll d_t$ represents the rank of the subspace.

The term $\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{x} + \boldsymbol{b} - \boldsymbol{U}\boldsymbol{x}$ represents the calculated intervention in the subspace, which is then projected back to the original space via $\boldsymbol{U}^{\intercal}$.

### 3. Hierarchical Integration of Editors
We will integrate $\psi$ into three distinct components of the LMM.

**A. Visual Representation Editing ($\psi_V$):**
We will insert distinct editors $\psi_v^i$ at the $i$-th layer of the vision encoder $\nu$. These editors will modify the hidden visual representations $T_{v,i}$ sequentially:
$$ T_{v,i} = \{ \psi_v^i(T_{v,i}^1), \psi_v^i(T_{v,i}^2), \dots, \psi_v^i(T_{v,i}^m) \} $$
This ensures that visual features are refined before cross-modal alignment.

**B. Cross-Modality Representation Editing ($\psi_c$):**
To enhance alignment between visual and textual features, we will apply an editor $\psi_c$ directly to the output of the cross-modality projector $\mathcal{C}$. The optimized visual embedding $X_v$ becomes:
$$ X_v = \psi_c(\mathcal{C}(\{T_v^1, \dots, T_v^m\})) $$

**C. Multimodal Representation Editing ($\psi_p, \psi_s$):**
Within the LLM $\tau$, we will strictly focus on editing the **textual-oriented** fraction of the multimodal representation. We will target $a$ prefix tokens and $b$ suffix tokens of the text embedding $X_t$, leaving the image tokens and the middle text tokens unaltered to preserve core semantic structure.

For the $j$-th layer of the LLM, we define editors $\psi_p^j$ (prefix) and $\psi_s^j$ (suffix). The layer input $X_j$ will be transformed as:
$$ X_j = \{ x_{v,j}^1, \dots, x_{v,j}^m, \underbrace{\psi_p^j(x_{t,j}^1, \dots, x_{t,j}^a)}_{\text{Edited Prefix}}, x_{t,j}^{a+1}, \dots, x_{t,j}^{n-b-1}, \underbrace{\psi_s^j(x_{t,j}^{n-b}, \dots, x_{t,j}^n)}_{\text{Edited Suffix}} \} $$

### 4. Controllability Mechanism
To enable explicit control, we will design the editors to perform targeted interventions. By training specific editors on counterfactual objectives (e.g., forcing a misclassification or alignment to a target class), we will manipulate the linear subspace of specific instrumental tokens (e.g., Region of Interest patches in $X_v$ or specific indicator tokens in $X_t$). This will allow us to verify if the model's decision-making can be steered via linear edits.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Extreme Parameter Efficiency:** We expect MRT to reduce the number of tunable parameters by orders of magnitude compared to LoRA and standard Adapters, while maintaining or exceeding performance.
2.  **Theoretical Advancement in LMM Tuning:** By proving the efficacy of linear representation editing in multimodal settings, we will shift the paradigm from weight-based tuning to representation-based tuning.
3.  **Interpretability and Control:** Unlike "black-box" prompt tuning, MRT will provide a mechanism for transparent, "white-box" control over model outputs, enabling precise behavior adjustment (e.g., counterfactual generation) through interpretable linear subspaces.

preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

preinstalled.zh: python:3.11 bookworm；上游代码按 PYTHONPATH 使用；pdflatex + bibtex；CPU 版 PyTorch 和 numpy、scipy、scikit-learn、pandas、matplotlib 等（constraints.txt 固定）
preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
